strengths: The paper presents a useful conceptual shift from per-scene semantic-feature optimization to mask lifting and direct matching. The combination of multi-granularity tracking, probabilistic 2D-to-3D grouping, boundary refinement, and VLM-derived textual hypotheses is coherent and relevant to open-vocabulary 3D understanding.

The reported accuracy is strong: 54.3 mIoU on LERF exceeds the best listed point-based baseline by 10.7 points and the best pixel-based baseline by 2.9 points. On the evaluated ScanNet settings, the method consistently improves both mIoU and mean accuracy.

The approach has attractive practical characteristics. It avoids semantic optimization, reports approximately 3 MB of feature storage and 8 GB peak VRAM, and directly produces groups of 3D Gaussians suitable for selection and interaction.

The feature-extraction ablation is informative: VLM-text matching reaches 54.3 mIoU versus 50.1 for filtered multi-view image matching, 39.2 for averaged features, and 36.9 for a single view. This supports the claim that textual distillation can mitigate view-dependent image-feature inconsistency.
The method is generally understandable, with helpful pipeline diagrams, mathematical definitions for mask lifting and entropy filtering, and quantitative evaluation on two distinct tasks.
weaknesses: A central efficiency claim is not adequately substantiated. The paper claims that adaptation falls from hours to minutes, but reports no end-to-end runtime for MUSplat, including SAM inference, DAM2SAM tracking at three granularities, periodic re-segmentation, Gaussian back-projection, and Gemini API calls. Table 1 only marks optimization time as “None,” which is not equivalent to measuring total processing time; the accounting of Dr.Splat's training time versus scene optimization is also unclear.

Reproducibility is materially limited. Numerical values or selection procedures are absent for the entropy, opacity, and semantic-similarity thresholds; the periodic detection interval, minimum-IoU rule, top-N view count, exact VLM prompt, decoding settings, CLIP backbone, SAM configuration, and visibility criterion are not specified. The exact ScanNet scenes, number of scenes, evaluation correspondence procedure, and treatment of overlapping groups are likewise not reported.

The comparison does not isolate the benefit of the proposed 3D machinery from that of a substantially stronger external semantic model. MUSplat uses the proprietary Gemini 2.5 Pro, whereas the baselines primarily rely on CLIP-derived features. No comparison uses the same VLM to relabel baseline groupings, and no alternative open VLM or repeated-run analysis is provided. Consequently, the source and robustness of the reported gains remain uncertain.

The claimed polysemous capability is not directly evaluated. Multiple candidate names and overlapping multi-granularity groups could support several concepts per Gaussian, but the experiments provide no multi-label or polysemy-specific benchmark, metric, or comparison against a monosemous variant. Standard object selection and semantic-class segmentation do not by themselves verify this central contribution.

The neutral-point model rests on insufficiently validated assumptions: projection disagreement is treated as boundary ambiguity without a precise treatment of occlusion, and low Gaussian opacity is assumed to indicate a semantically neutral transition rather than a valid surface element. Its ablation is limited to LERF and yields only a 1.3-point total gain, with no threshold sensitivity, boundary metric, or visualization of identified neutral points.

Evaluation breadth and protocol clarity are insufficient for the strength of the general claims. LERF contains only four scenes, the evaluated ScanNet subset is unspecified, and there are no variance estimates or robustness studies for tracking failures and VLM label errors. The assertion that downstream modules “gracefully” handle mask and re-identification artifacts is not experimentally tested.

There are methodological ambiguities that affect reproducibility and interpretation. Section 3 selects every candidate above a similarity threshold and unions the associated groups, while the object-selection protocol describes choosing the most similar instance or instances. The paper also calls the approach “training-free” despite requiring a pre-trained, scene-specific 3DGS; “no additional semantic training” would be more precise. Overall, the results are promising enough to place the work near the acceptance boundary, but the missing protocol details, unequal semantic-model comparison, and lack of evidence for the polysemy claim prevent a weak-accept recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and proposes a conceptually simple pipeline combining multi-view mask tracking, probabilistic mask lifting, boundary filtering, and language-based instance retrieval.

The reported results are promising: MUSplat obtains 54.3 mean mIoU on LERF and consistently leads the listed point-based methods on the ScanNet class subsets. The feature-extraction ablation also shows a substantial improvement from VLM-generated names over direct CLIP image matching.

Avoiding scene-specific semantic optimization could be practically useful. Representing overlapping object groups can naturally associate a Gaussian with multiple concepts, and the method is compatible with an existing 3DGS reconstruction.

The main pipeline and mask-lifting equations are generally easy to follow, and the paper includes useful component ablations. weaknesses: The central open-vocabulary and polysemy claims are not adequately demonstrated. Retrieval is restricted to the finite set of names that Gemini happens to generate for each group; a valid query cannot be recovered if the relevant attribute or concept is absent from that set. No experiment explicitly measures polysemous membership, attribute queries, vocabulary coverage, or performance on concepts omitted by the generated candidates.

It is unclear how much of the improvement comes from the proposed 3D machinery rather than from replacing CLIP image matching with a powerful proprietary VLM that directly names benchmark objects. Table 5 confirms that this substitution accounts for most of the measured gain, but there are no comparisons across VLMs, no oracle-name baseline, and no analysis of label coverage or hallucination. Thus the evidence does not isolate the claimed semantic-distillation contribution.

The experiments are insufficiently specified for verification or reproduction. The paper omits the SAM variant and settings, number and spacing of frames, periodic detection interval, track association procedure, top-N value, exact VLM prompt and decoding/API configuration, CLIP variant, and all reported thresholds (tau_h, tau_alpha, eta). It also does not identify the ScanNet scenes, sample count, or precise Gaussian-to-ground-truth point correspondence and evaluation procedure.

The efficiency comparison does not substantiate the headline claim of reducing adaptation from hours to minutes. No end-to-end runtime is reported for SAM mask generation, three-granularity DAM2SAM tracking, mask lifting, rendering, or Gemini calls. Table 1 instead mixes optimization time, CLIP-feature storage, and grouping VRAM, without hardware or measurement protocol; it also labels Dr.Splat as requiring no scene optimization while assigning it about one hour of training time.

The neutral-point argument is technically under-justified. Learned Gaussian opacity is not inherently a reliable discriminator between anti-aliasing Gaussians and valid surface Gaussians, and center projection without a clearly defined visibility or occlusion test can itself create cross-view disagreement. The only evidence is a small LERF ablation: entropy filtering adds 0.2 mIoU and the full module adds 1.3 over the unfiltered model.

Evaluation breadth and reporting are too weak for the size of the claims. LERF contains only four scenes, ScanNet evaluation uses an unspecified subset, no uncertainty or per-scene ScanNet results are given, and robustness to tracking errors and VLM failures is asserted rather than tested. The qualitative evidence is also limited to a few small examples.

The novelty relative to the closest mask-lifting and segmentation approaches is not established. FlashSplat and Segment-then-Splat appear only in the references and are neither technically contrasted nor experimentally compared. Much of the pipeline otherwise consists of existing SAM/DAM2SAM tracking, standard alpha-weighted back-projection, threshold filtering, VLM naming, and CLIP text similarity.

Several claims are overstated or imprecise. The stated 10.7-point LERF improvement applies only against the best listed point-based baseline; against the best listed method overall, the mean improvement is 2.9 points. The paper also describes its output as an uncompressed CLIP representation even though it actually reduces observations to VLM-generated names and CLIP text embeddings. These issues affect interpretation of the contribution, not merely presentation polish.

strengths: MUSplat offers a useful change of paradigm: it avoids per-scene semantic-feature optimization by lifting tracked 2D masks into overlapping 3D Gaussian groups and associating these groups with VLM-generated textual descriptions. This naturally permits a Gaussian to participate in multiple concepts and is practically attractive for interactive 3D understanding.

The reported results are strong across two tasks. MUSplat reaches 54.3 mean IoU on the four LERF scenes, exceeding the best listed point-based baseline by 10.7 points and the best pixel-based baseline by 2.9 points. On ScanNet, it consistently leads the listed methods for all 19-, 15-, and 10-class settings, reaching 45.5, 47.2, and 53.7 mIoU respectively.

The feature-extraction ablation provides useful evidence for the main design choice: VLM-text matching obtains 54.3 mIoU, compared with 36.9 for a single image feature, 39.2 for averaged image features, and 50.1 for filtered image features. This supports the claim that textual distillation can reduce multi-view feature inconsistency.

The method combines conceptually simple components into a coherent pipeline. Contribution-weighted mask lifting is compatible with 3DGS rendering, while the entropy-and-opacity mechanism explicitly addresses uncertain boundaries. The complete neutral-point procedure improves LERF mIoU from 53.0 to 54.3.

The stated efficiency improvements are substantial: approximately 3 MB of semantic-feature storage and 8 GB peak grouping VRAM, versus roughly 3 GB and 20–26 GB for several listed feature-based approaches. The manuscript is generally clear, and its diagrams communicate the pipeline effectively.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is presently inadequate. The manuscript does not report the numerical values of the supposedly fixed entropy, opacity, and matching thresholds; the number of VLM views N; the CLIP and SAM variants; the periodic re-detection interval and IoU criterion; or sufficient tracking, prompting, decoding, and 3DGS configuration details. The exact ScanNet scenes and categories are also referenced only indirectly through OpenGaussian.

The headline efficiency claim is incompletely supported. Table 1 reports no training time for MUSplat but does not give end-to-end runtime for SAM mask generation, DAM2SAM tracking, multi-view back-projection, or Gemini inference. Consequently, the abstract's claim that adaptation takes only minutes cannot be verified, and labeling the method's time as 'None' obscures nontrivial preprocessing and proprietary API costs.

The claimed polysemous capability is not directly evaluated. The benchmarks primarily measure conventional object or class selection, with no controlled experiments on overlapping semantic concepts such as object identity, material, attribute, part, and superclass queries. Overlapping multi-granularity groups make polysemy plausible, but do not establish that it works reliably.

Most of the performance gain comes from Gemini 2.5 Pro, a powerful proprietary and potentially stochastic external model, yet there is no comparison across VLMs, repeated-run analysis, API/version specification, or evaluation of labeling failures. Comparisons against baselines that do not use an analogous VLM also leave unclear how much of the improvement derives from the proposed 3D method rather than stronger external semantic supervision.

The evaluation is fairly narrow: LERF contains only four scenes, while the ScanNet protocol lacks per-scene results, variance, and robustness analysis. There are no experiments quantifying sensitivity to thresholds, tracking errors, segmentation-mask quality, view count, or incomplete visibility, despite the pipeline depending heavily on these factors.

The neutral-point rationale is only partially justified. It assumes that ambiguous boundary Gaussians have low opacity, while semantic entropy is computed from projected Gaussian centers; the manuscript does not define visibility handling sufficiently or analyze occlusion and extended Gaussian footprints. The modest 1.3-point total gain supports usefulness but not the broader characterization of such points as semantically neutral.

Some claims should be stated more precisely. The reported 10.7-point LERF advantage applies to the listed point-based methods, not to the best method overall, where the margin is 2.9 points. Likewise, calling MUSplat training-free should be qualified as requiring a separately trained 3DGS representation and multiple pretrained foundation models.

strengths: The central object-centric design is intuitive and potentially useful: geometry remains unchanged while overlapping Gaussian groups are associated with lightweight textual hypotheses, enabling direct 3D querying and supporting part/object memberships.

The method is technically coherent and mostly specified clearly, including contribution-weighted back-projection, entropy/opacity boundary filtering, query matching, thresholds, the VLM prompt, and evaluation scenes. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/f1f05d030c02493d8d18b01a6f2cc2ca/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Results on the 10 evaluated ScanNet scenes are strong: the reported 45.5 mIoU for 19 classes exceeds the best listed baseline by 4.8 points, with consistent gains for the 15- and 10-class settings.

The method offers an attractive accuracy-efficiency trade-off. The reported end-to-end scene adaptation time is about 9.25 minutes, and avoiding per-Gaussian CLIP features plausibly reduces memory and feature-storage requirements substantially.

The paper includes useful component ablations, threshold sensitivity analysis, runtime decomposition, alternative VLMs, sparse-view experiments, and explicit failure cases. Presentation and qualitative results are generally clear.
weaknesses: The headline performance claim is overstated. On LERF, 54.3 mIoU is 3.9 points above only the other listed training-free 3D method, but is below LAGA by 9.7 points and below several 2D methods. Calling this an unqualified new SOTA, as done in the text, is not supported by Table 2.

The storage claim does not measure the complete extrinsic representation. Table 1 reports only 'CLIP feature storage' (3 MB), while the proposed layer must also store potentially overlapping Gaussian-index sets for every object group, textual hypotheses, and possibly tracking products. Because overlap can duplicate many indices, total semantic-layer storage and its scaling with scene/group complexity are necessary to substantiate the claimed orders-of-magnitude reduction.

The strongest semantic results depend on proprietary Gemini 2.5 Pro, whose exact version, decoding configuration, stochastic variability, API environment, and cost are not reported. Table 9 states that all timings are measured on a V100 even though Gemini inference is externally hosted, making the runtime comparison insufficiently controlled and difficult to reproduce.

The claimed native support for rich polysemy is not directly validated. There is no quantitative polysemy benchmark or ablation comparing overlapping multi-granularity groups against disjoint/single-granularity groups. Figure 13 appears to count memberships produced by the method itself, so it is not independent evidence of semantic correctness.

The novelty is moderate: the system combines existing SAM/DAM2SAM masks, contribution-weighted back-projection, heuristic boundary filtering, VLM object naming, and CLIP text matching. The paper frames this as a new paradigm, but does not adequately compare with prior object-/instance-level indexing or clarify which empirical gains come specifically from decoupling rather than stronger VLM classification.

The 'neutral point' interpretation is insufficiently justified. Low opacity plus cross-view label disagreement does not establish that a Gaussian has no semantic identity; it can also indicate occlusion, mask error, thin geometry, or view-dependent reconstruction artifacts. The full heuristic improves LERF by only 1.3 mIoU over initial grouping, so claims that it guarantees precise boundaries or that both stages are essential are too strong.

Important evaluation details remain ambiguous: the object-selection description alternates between selecting the most similar instances and thresholding at 0.9; visibility/occlusion handling in the entropy calculation is unclear; and there are no repeated VLM runs or uncertainty estimates. These issues materially affect reproducibility and interpretation, though they appear correctable.

strengths: The object-centric semantic index is a useful engineering direction: it separates semantic metadata from 3DGS parameters, permits overlapping part/object groups, and avoids scene-specific semantic optimization.
The reported ScanNet results are strong under the paper's protocol: 45.5 mIoU for 19 classes versus 40.7 for the strongest listed baseline, with consistent gains for the 15- and 10-class settings.

The paper includes informative component studies. VLM text distillation improves LERF mIoU from 50.1 to 54.3 over the strongest CLIP-image alternative, while threshold and VLM-backbone studies expose meaningful dependencies.
The main pipeline is understandable, and the supplement provides the prompt, thresholds, evaluated ScanNet scenes and categories, failure cases, and a component-wise runtime breakdown.
weaknesses: The state-of-the-art claim for LERF is misleading. The proposed method obtains 54.3 mean mIoU in Table 2, substantially below Occam's LGS (61.3), 3DVLGS (62.0), and LAGA (64.0). The claimed 3.9-point advantage holds only within the narrowly defined '3D training-free' subgroup and does not support the manuscript's unqualified SOTA language.

The headline storage and efficiency comparison is not adequately supported. Table 1 reports only 'CLIP feature storage,' not total semantic-index storage; the proposed representation must also store potentially overlapping sets of Gaussian indices for every object group, but their size is omitted. Likewise, the 8 GB VRAM and nine-minute runtime do not account for the compute and memory of the remotely hosted Gemini 2.5 Pro model, making comparisons with locally executed baselines inequitable.

The central 'neutral point' interpretation is weakly justified. Cross-view mask-label entropy can arise from occlusion, tracking errors, center projection, or inaccurate masks, while low Gaussian opacity is not demonstrated to imply an object-neutral boundary element. There is no ground-truth evaluation of neutral-point detection or boundary accuracy, and the entire module improves LERF mIoU by only 1.3 points (53.0 to 54.3).

The claimed open-vocabulary capability is constrained by proposal and vocabulary bottlenecks: an entity must first be proposed and tracked by SAM/DAM2SAM, and each group is reduced to only five VLM-generated nouns. No evaluation addresses attributes, relations, affordances, unseen query formulations, missing proposals, or concepts not covered by those nouns, so claims of rich polysemy and arbitrary-language understanding are overstated.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the reported gains. The manuscript does not identify the exact SAM or CLIP variants, Gemini API/version and decoding settings, random seeds, repeated-run variance, or the generated hypotheses. Closed, potentially changing VLM outputs are central to performance, as Table 6 itself shows a 7.3-point range across VLMs.

The query protocol is ambiguous and insufficiently analyzed. The main text describes selecting the most similar instance(s), whereas the supplement uses a fixed cosine threshold of 0.9 with an any-of-five rule. There is no sensitivity study for this decisive threshold or explanation of how no-match and multiple-match cases are handled during scoring.

Evaluation breadth is modest—four LERF scenes and ten ScanNet scenes—and the additional real-world and GraspNet evidence is qualitative only. The paper provides no uncertainty estimates, repeated VLM trials, quantitative boundary metrics, total storage measurements, or controlled end-to-end runtime comparisons.

Overall, the object-centric design and ScanNet numbers are worthwhile, but the unsupported efficiency accounting, misleading SOTA framing, weak validation of the main neutral-point concept, and substantial reproducibility gaps presently outweigh those merits.

strengths: The central design is useful and reasonably original: semantics are represented by overlapping object-level groups and textual hypotheses rather than one feature vector per Gaussian. This naturally permits part/object overlap and avoids modifying the underlying 3DGS representation.

The pipeline is technically coherent. It combines multi-view mask tracking, contribution-weighted back-projection, entropy/opacity boundary filtering, and VLM-based naming into a practical training-free system.

The ScanNet results are compelling: ExtrinSplat obtains 45.5/47.2/53.7 mIoU for 19/15/10 classes, consistently exceeding the strongest listed baselines while also achieving the best reported mean accuracy.

The paper provides useful ablations for feature extraction, VLM choice, number of textual hypotheses, neutral-point thresholds, and sparse mask supervision. The component-wise runtime analysis and explicit failure cases further strengthen the empirical presentation.

The method is practically attractive: the reported end-to-end adaptation time is approximately 9.25 minutes, and the semantic feature storage is only about 3 MB. The manuscript is generally clear, well illustrated, and includes concrete thresholds, prompts, evaluated scenes, and implementation details. weaknesses: The LERF performance claim is materially overstated. The reported mean of 54.3 is below LaGa (64.0), 3DVLGS (62.0), and Occam's LGS (61.3); the stated 3.9-point improvement applies only relative to LUDVIG within the restricted 3D training-free subgroup. Broad claims of a new SOTA or outperforming embedding-based frameworks should be qualified accordingly.

The efficiency comparison does not establish total system cost fairly. Table 1 reports only 'CLIP feature storage,' apparently excluding the overlapping Gaussian-index sets that constitute the proposed semantic layer, as well as intermediate masks and tracking data. Peak VRAM also excludes the external compute used by Gemini, while baseline measurements and hardware/protocol provenance are insufficiently specified.

Reproducibility is limited by reliance on the proprietary Gemini 2.5 Pro service. The exact model snapshot, decoding settings, randomness, API cost, and handling of malformed or variable responses are not reported. The runtime measured on a V100 is also ambiguous because a major stage is externally hosted VLM inference.

Two central conceptual claims receive limited direct support. There is no ablation comparing overlapping multi-granularity groups against disjoint or single-granularity groups on explicitly polysemous queries. Likewise, 'neutral points' are not validated against ground truth; low opacity and cross-view disagreement can also arise from reconstruction, calibration, occlusion, or mask errors. The complete neutral-point module improves LERF mIoU by 1.3 points, which supports the heuristic but not the stronger ontological or guarantee-style claims.

Evaluation remains fairly narrow: four LERF scenes and ten ScanNet scenes, without per-scene variation, repeated VLM trials, uncertainty estimates, or sensitivity analysis for the query threshold. Important ScanNet details—Gaussian-to-ground-truth correspondence, treatment of unmatched/neutral points, and whether all baselines use exactly the same reconstruction constraints—are not sufficiently documented. These are material evidence limitations, though the strong results and ablations still leave the balance favorable for acceptance.

Several statements should be moderated as presentation refinements: the method does not 'guarantee' precise semantics, its grouping is primarily mask tracking and back-projection rather than unconstrained 3D clustering, and the semantic-feature consistency discussion does not by itself demonstrate that textual hypotheses are universally more stable.
